content: Infections associated with the use of intravascular catheters, particularly bloodstream infections (BSIs), are largely preventable if proper precautions and practices are followed during catheter insertion, maintenance, access, and removal. This holds true regardless of a country’s income level. Intravascular catheters are broadly categorized into two types: those inserted into peripheral blood vessels (veins and arteries) and those inserted into central vessels. Peripheral intravenous catheters (PIVCs) are among the most commonly used invasive devices in healthcare settings, with up to 70% of hospitalized patients requiring a PIVC during their stay. Consequently, the global burden of BSIs and related infections associated with PIVCs is significant. Peripheral inserted central catheters (PICCs) are less frequently used than PIVCs, but their placement in large central veins increases the risk of systemic bloodstream infections if they become infected. Peripheral arterial catheters (PACs) are primarily used in intensive care units for continuous blood pressure monitoring and arterial blood sampling to guide ventilation management. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed guidelines to prevent infections associated with intravascular catheters. Part 1 of these guidelines focuses on best practices for preventing BSIs and other infections related to peripherally inserted IV catheters, including PIVCs, PICCs, and PACs, across all patient populations (adults, adolescents, children, and neonates) in various healthcare settings. Part 2, to be released in 2024, will address centrally inserted intravascular catheters. The guidelines emphasize evidence-based approaches to catheter management, including insertion, maintenance, access, and removal. They are intended for clinicians such as doctors, nurses, and infection prevention and control (IPC) professionals, as well as hospital administrators and patients. The goal is to ensure adherence to safe practices and provide appropriate support for clinicians. The development of these recommendations followed a rigorous methodology, including systematic reviews of scientific evidence, stakeholder input, and the use of the GRADE framework to assess the balance of benefits and risks. The guidelines are structured into six key sections: education and hand hygiene, insertion, maintenance, access, removal, and catheter choice. Key recommendations include: 1. Clinicians should be educated on the indications for catheter use, proper procedures, and infection control measures. 2. Regular assessment of clinicians’ knowledge and adherence to guidelines is essential. 3. Hand hygiene and aseptic no-touch techniques should be rigorously followed. 4. Sterile techniques should be used for PICC and PAC insertion, while PIVC insertion may not require sterile gloves if aseptic techniques are strictly adhered to. 5. Skin disinfection prior to catheter insertion is critical. 6. Standardized insertion kits should be used for PICC and PAC placement, and their use is suggested for PIVC insertion. 7. Ultrasound guidance is recommended for PICC insertion but not routinely for PIVC placement. 8. For PIVC insertion, distal arm veins are preferred over proximal veins, and upper limb sites are preferred over lower limb sites. 9. For neonates, upper limb sites are preferred for PICC insertion, and scalp veins should generally be avoided for PIVC and PICC placement. 10. Catheter maintenance should include sterile dressing protocols and regular flushing with sterile fluids. 11. Administration sets should be changed on a regular schedule. 12. Catheter access should follow sterile or aseptic protocols, and closed-access hub systems may be used. These guidelines aim to provide a practical framework for the safe use of intravascular catheters, minimizing the risk of BSIs and other infections.
